summary:
TwinGround is a bilingual web platform that finds Earth analogs for any location on the Moon or Mars while quantifying what Earth cannot replicate. Users pick a 20, 40, or 80 km window on a 3D globe, describe a site in plain language, or upload a terrain image. TwinGround harmonizes NASA orbital data (LRO, Lunar Prospector, Mars Odyssey, MGS, MRO) in units, scale, and sensing depth, ranking 484,015 Earth windows across ten mission facets and operational uses: ISRU resources, mobility, thermal work, base siting, and lava-tube search.   


Backed by our pre-registered study (The Earth Ceiling), TwinGround computes the highest match score any measured terrestrial site can reach, achieving 0.52–0.77 retrieval efficiency versus -0.19–0.02 for traditional screening. Users can compare 3D terrains side by side, inspect site dossiers (geology, access, field season), walk either world under true gravity, and ask a fine-tuned Llama 3.2 1B assistant for cited explanations.   


Because sites chosen merely by appearance bias toward continental crust, TwinGround replaces guesswork with a reproducible boundary-condition inventory—telling teams what to test in the field versus in simulants or thermal-vacuum chambers for Artemis and Mars missions.

1. Project Overview: What TwinGround Does & How It Works

TwinGround is a web platform engineered to identify and evaluate terrestrial analogs for any target location on the Moon or Mars while rigorously quantifying what Earth cannot replicate. Users can select a square analysis window (20, 40, or 80 km on a side) directly on a 3D planetary globe or describe desired site conditions in natural language. TwinGround extracts the query window’s physical and geochemical properties from harmonized NASA orbital datasets and ranks Earth candidates from an index of 484,015 land windows (compared at the same window size) across ten mission facets for four operational uses, ISRU feedstock resources, surface mobility, thermal environment, and base siting, plus a dedicated lava-tube search.

Rather than presenting a black-box score, every candidate site is accompanied by:

  1. Property-level explainability: A transparent breakdown of which parameters match within tolerance, which diverge, and which lie outside Earth’s natural envelope.
  2. Side-by-side 3D terrain comparison: Co-registered elevation meshes draped with orbital and terrestrial imagery.
  3. A comprehensive site dossier: Aridity, lithology, testable mission operations, optimal field season, and logistics (nearest road, town, and airport).
  4. An interactive Astronaut Explorer: A first- and third-person 3D environment allowing users to traverse both the planetary target and its Earth analog under true local gravity.
  5. The Ask AI Assistant: A fine-tuned Llama 3.2 1B model trained on 10,220 dialogues and grounded in our research paper and its cited literature, answering methodological questions and explaining candidate rankings with verifiable citations.
  6. Game Mode: A guided mission experience featuring a commander’s video briefing, voiced radio instructions over the live interface, field tasks in the Astronaut Explorer, and a mission debrief.

The study maps 117 lunar and Martian query windows and 75,860 terrestrial windows (40 km scale) into a unified property space harmonized in measurement units, spatial support, and sensing depth, defining the Earth ceiling as the highest use score any measured terrestrial window can attain. Every confirmatory statistical test was locked with a SHA-256 hash prior to inspecting the corresponding Earth evaluation data.

  • 484,015 indexed Earth land windows (20 / 40 / 80 km)
  • 117 lunar and Martian query windows evaluated
  • 0.52–0.77 retrieval efficiency of property-based ranking (lunar FeO, K, Th)
  • -0.19–0.02 retrieval efficiency of traditional setting-based screening
Key Findings
  • Terrain roughness is universally matchable: Kilometre-scale surface roughness can be replicated on Earth for every target tested, yielding a mobility ceiling of 1.0 across all 117 queries.
  • Surface geochemistry and extreme cold face hard terrestrial limits: No Earth regolith window simultaneously matches lunar FeO, TiO₂, K, and Th (mean lunar resource ceiling: 0.75). Martian FeO exceeds every measured Earth topsoil footprint (52 of 52 queries), and for 8 of 18 named Martian sites, no terrestrial surface comes within 20 K of modelled nighttime temperatures.
  • Qualitative screening introduces systematic compositional bias: Selecting analogs by environmental setting (“arid, bare, basaltic”) successfully enriches for traditional catalogued analog sites (~ 12.2× higher density), but systematically shifts candidates toward potassium- and thorium-rich continental crust—away from lunar and Martian geochemistry—across all 20 distinct candidate pools tested.
  • A boundary-condition inventory guides mission testing (Table 6): TwinGround allocates terrain validation to Earth field sites, geochemical feedstock testing to laboratory simulants, and extreme radiative/thermal regimes to thermal-vacuum chambers. Mobility and trafficability trials can rely on field sites selected by measured roughness (ceiling = 1.0). Conversely, lunar mare feedstock (ceiling = 0.40, lacking mare-level Ti and Fe) requires simulants, while Martian nights below ≈ 185 K and lunar polar illumination and cold traps require specialized thermal and thermal-vacuum facilities.

2. The Problem

NASA’s Artemis program aims to establish a sustained human presence near the lunar south pole as a stepping stone toward crewed Mars exploration. Prior to flight, rovers, excavators, in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) plants, habitats, and crews must undergo rigorous terrestrial testing. For decades, terrestrial analog sites have underpinned this preparation through functional inference: a site serves as an analog specifically for the physical or chemical parameters a given test depends upon. A basaltic lava flow may accurately replicate rover mobility conditions while differing substantially from the regolith feedstock chemistry required for an ISRU trial, and neither may reproduce the thermal environment a surface habitat must endure.

Historically, analog selection has relied on expert familiarity and curated catalogues such as NASA’s Planetary Analog Explorer, which categorize sites by qualitative setting descriptors—arid, unvegetated, basaltic, volcanic, or cold. Canonical examples include the Atacama Desert, Hawaiian volcanoes, and the McMurdo Dry Valleys for Mars, alongside young basaltic fields such as Craters of the Moon for lunar mare terrain. While qualitative selection offers practical advantages (established logistics, prior baseline studies, and multiple co-located features), it has never provided quantitative answers to two foundational questions:

  1. How closely does a candidate Earth site reproduce the measured properties of a specific lunar or Martian target?
  2. What is the upper bound on how closely any location on Earth could reproduce them?

Answering these questions presents a fundamental multi-scale challenge. Lunar and Martian elemental abundances derive from orbital gamma-ray spectrometers whose footprints span tens to hundreds of kilometres, whereas terrestrial geochemical data come from airborne radiometric surveys, soil cores, and hand-specimen rock analyses spanning centimetres to kilometres. Topography, albedo, and surface temperature similarly vary in spatial resolution, solar illumination, and local acquisition time. TwinGround resolves this harmonization gap first, then ranks candidates and explains the physical limits of each match.

Our study addresses three core research questions:

  • RQ1 — Feasibility and its bound: Does Earth contain spatial windows that reproduce lunar and Martian composition and physical environments under multi-property, same-unit constraints, and what physical mechanisms limit the best attainable match?
  • RQ2 — Validity of heuristic analogs: Do candidates selected via qualitative setting criteria approach this terrestrial bound, or are they systematically displaced?
  • RQ3 — Generalizability: How accurately can unmeasured Earth geochemistry be predicted from environmental covariates, and how do analog match rates vary across spatial scales?

x = (FeO, TiO₂, K, Th, albedo, roughness, T_day, T_night)

3.2 Spatial Harmonization and Multiscale Discretization

Targets and terrestrial candidates are defined as square tangent-plane windows of side length L ∈ {20, 40, 80} km and are compared strictly at equal L. The global Earth index encompasses every ETOPO 2022 land window containing at most 5% ocean area: 484,015 windows (326,374 at 20 km, 75,860 at 40 km, and 81,781 at 80 km), spanning latitudes up to ≈ 84° N–S. The 117 planetary query windows comprise 37 named mission-relevant sites (19 lunar—including 6 south-polar windows selected from LOLA illumination maps—and 18 Martian) plus 80 windows sampled uniformly at random prior to examining any property values (40 on the Moon within 60° of the equator, and 40 on Mars within 55°).

Although orbital and airborne gamma-ray spectrometers both sense the upper few tens of centimetres in identical units, their spatial footprints differ by orders of magnitude. Terrestrial grids are therefore convolved with the spatial response kernel of the corresponding orbital instrument prior to comparison:

x̄ₖ(w) = Σᵢ K(dᵢ) · xₖ(sᵢ) / Σᵢ K(dᵢ), K_Moon(d) = exp(−d² / 2σ²), K_Mars(d) = 𝟙[d ≤ 220 km] (1)

where xₖ(sᵢ) denotes grid values at distance dᵢ from the window centre w. The lunar kernel is a Gaussian with a 45 km full width at half maximum (matching a Lunar Prospector measurement at 30 km altitude), truncated at 3σ; the Martian kernel is a 220 km disk representing the half-signal radius of Mars Odyssey. A window is deemed valid when at least 80% of the kernel weight contains unmasked measurements (9,904 windows under the lunar kernel and 8,079 under the Martian kernel).

To quantify sub-footprint heterogeneity masked by orbital averaging, we repeated the comparison across a ladder of spatial supports: native airborne radiometric grids sampled on a 1 km lattice and aggregated into blocks of 1, 2, 4, 8, 20, and 40 km, alongside individual whole-rock geochemical analyses representing hand specimens.

3.3 Dual-Track Geochemical Representation: Regolith and Bedrock

Terrestrial geochemistry enters the framework along two complementary tracks that reflect distinct geological sampling regimes:

  • Regolith track: Combines airborne gamma-ray K and Th (Australia and North America), which sense the same upper few tens of centimetres as the orbital instruments, with topsoil FeO and TiO₂ (USGS, NGSA, FOREGS) sampled from the upper 5–25 cm. This track captures the weathered surface mantle averaged by orbital footprints and encountered directly by rovers and excavators.
  • Bedrock track: Computes the median of at least three GEOROC whole-rock analyses of subaerial volcanic or plutonic lithologies within each window, drawn from 339,587 curated analyses. This track characterizes unweathered rock as exposed in outcrops and hand specimens.

Of the 75,860 Earth windows at 40 km, 4,610 have measured topsoil FeO, 4,165 possess unattenuated airborne K and Th, and 6,172 contain whole-rock FeO, TiO₂, K, and Th; 616 windows share FeO measurements across both tracks, and 88 contain all four elements on both tracks, enabling direct co-located comparisons between weathered surface material and underlying bedrock. Albedo, roughness, and surface temperature are shared across both tracks. For petrological reference, 923 whole-rock analyses of Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, and 17 basalts were incorporated from the Astromat lunar sample synthesis.

4. Theoretical Foundation

4.1 Problem Formulation

Given a planetary query window q with property vector x_q, a set of candidate Earth windows E, and an operational use u ∈ {resources, mobility, thermal, base siting}, we seek: (i) a ranking of E according to how well each window satisfies the physical and chemical requirements of u, and (ii) the maximum score attainable by any measured terrestrial window. A property match is defined by a physical tolerance τₖ, fixed prior to reading any Earth data: FeO ± 3 wt%, TiO₂ ± 1.5 wt%, K ± 0.2 wt%, Th ± 2 ppm, albedo ± 0.05, roughness ± 1°, and temperature ± 20 K.

4.2 Match Probability

For a query q, an Earth window e, and property k, the match probability pₖ(q, e) is defined as:

pₖ(q, e) = 𝟙[ |qₖ − eₖ| ≤ τₖ ] (measured)

pₖ(q, e) = Φ((qₖ + τₖ − μₖ) / σₖ) − Φ((qₖ − τₖ − μₖ) / σₖ) (estimated) (2)

Measured values enter via a binary indicator function, whereas estimated values enter via a Gaussian predictive distribution with mean μₖ and scale σₖ = (uₖ - lₖ) / (2 z_0.95) derived from their 90% conformal prediction interval [lₖ, uₖ]. Uncertain estimates thus receive calibrated partial credit proportional to their probability mass within tolerance.

4.3 Use Score and the Earth Ceiling

The composite use score Sᵤ(q, e) and the Earth ceiling Cᵤ(q) are computed as:

Sᵤ(q, e) = Σ_{k ∈ Kᵤ(q)} wᵤ,ₖ · pₖ(q, e) / Σ_{k ∈ Kᵤ(q)} wᵤ,ₖ, Cᵤ(q) = max_{e ∈ E_meas} Sᵤ(q, e) (3)

where Kᵤ(q) denotes the subset of use-relevant properties available for query q, and E_meas is the set of Earth windows with direct measurements. A ceiling of 1.0 indicates that at least one measured terrestrial window falls within tolerance across every required property. A ceiling below 1.0 stems from one of three causes: a composition unattainable in any terrestrial window, a thermal or radiative regime absent on Earth, or individual properties that occur separately on Earth but never co-occur within the same window.

To ensure our findings are not artifacts of specific parameter choices, every Earth ceiling was recomputed across 1,000 random weight vectors per query and use (sampled from a unit-concentration Dirichlet distribution) and under tolerances scaled by factors of 0.5, 1.5, and 2.0.

4.4 Retrieval Efficiency

To benchmark candidate ranking algorithms against held-out terrestrial measurements, we define retrieval efficiency (RE) as:

RE = (Ḡ − R̄) / (Ū − R̄) (4)

where Ḡ is the mean fraction of a method’s top 30 spatially distinct candidates (centres separated by at least 1.5 L) that fall within tolerance on held-out measured values, R̄ is the expected fraction under random ordering, and Ū is the upper bound achieved by an oracle ranking directly on the held-out measurements. RE = 0 corresponds to random selection, while RE = 1 represents optimal measurement-guided retrieval.

4.5 Heuristic Setting-Based Screening (Baseline)

To model conventional analog selection practice, the geological and environmental context of each planetary query was encoded as qualitative criteria derived from orbital maps—mirroring expert site descriptions. Lunar settings were extracted from the USGS Unified Geologic Map and Lunar Prospector FeO classifications; Martian settings were derived from the USGS global geologic map, SWIM ground-ice indicators, and OMEGA/CRISM mineralogical descriptors. These criteria (aridity, bare ground, cold temperature, permafrost, basaltic or sedimentary lithology, proximity to basaltic volcanoes, aeolian or hydrated settings, and low solar elevation) were evaluated across Earth using GLiM, WorldCover, Köppen–Geiger, the Global Aridity Index, SoilGrids, and the Smithsonian volcano catalogue. Each criterion yields a score of 1 (match), 0.5 (partial), or 0 (mismatch); their mean defines the setting fit F(e), and windows with F(e) ≥ 0.75 form the heuristic candidate pool. Crucially, this screening uses no geochemical, albedo, or roughness data, enabling an unconfounded evaluation against those independent properties.

4.6 Estimating Unmeasured Earth Geochemistry

Because direct geochemical surveys cover a limited fraction of Earth’s land surface, we trained gradient-boosted decision trees with 90% conformal prediction intervals to estimate K, Th, FeO, and TiO₂ from chemistry-free environmental covariates (lithology, land cover, climate, soil texture, cation exchange capacity, relief, surface temperature, albedo, terrain morphology, and spectral reflectance). Two validation regimes were tested: spatial interpolation (withholding labels within 100 km of each test window) and cross-continental transfer (holding out an entire continent). On identical cross-validation folds, gradient-boosted trees were benchmarked against covariate-space k-nearest neighbours, inverse-distance weighting, and spatial Gaussian processes.

4.7 Pre-Registration and Statistical Rigor

For every confirmatory experiment, query targets, candidate pools, test statistics, and decision thresholds were documented in a protocol file whose SHA-256 hash was recorded prior to accessing any Earth evaluation data, preventing post-hoc tuning of hypotheses or candidate sets. Heuristic screening was evaluated via match-rate differences against random windows, one-sided permutation tests, two-stage cluster bootstrap confidence intervals, and exact sign-flip tests across distinct pools, alongside an Earth-to-Earth positive control. All machine-learning models were trained using a single fixed random seed. Exploratory analyses added after inspecting results (including the Earth-ceiling synthesis itself) are explicitly designated as post hoc.

Candidate windows are scored on both regolith and bedrock tracks (Eqs. 2–3) and evaluated via the Earth ceiling, held-out retrieval efficiency (Eq. 4), heuristic screening benchmarks, and spatial scale/transfer analyses. — insert image images/03_framework.png here if the editor allows]

5. Results

5.1 The Earth Ceiling at Regolith and Bedrock Scales

Single-property physical uses are universally satisfiable on Earth: every planetary query finds terrestrial windows within tolerance on kilometre-scale roughness, yielding a mobility ceiling of 1.0 across all 117 queries. Geochemistry, however, is sharply bounded. No lunar query achieves a regolith resource ceiling of 1.0 (mean: 0.75). For Mars, the mean regolith resource ceiling drops to 0.61, and no Martian query reaches 1.0 for thermal environment (mean: 0.56) or base siting (mean: 0.75). Across the 71 use ceilings below 1.0 among named targets, 18 are constrained by an unattainable composition, 16 by an absent thermal or radiative regime, and 37 by properties that never co-occur within the same terrestrial window.

On the bedrock track, mean resource ceilings rise to 0.98 (Moon) and 0.995 (Mars), yet qualifying windows remain exceedingly rare: a median of 41 out of 6,172 whole-rock windows (0.66%) for lunar queries and just 6 (0.10%) for Martian queries. Thus, while comparable compositions exist in Earth’s geological record, they occur as localized rock outcrops rather than the continuous regolith mantles sampled by orbital footprints and traversed by surface missions.

5.2 Regolith vs. Bedrock: Two Sources of the Chemical Shortfall

Within the 616 co-located windows measured on both tracks, terrestrial topsoil contains a median of 3.6 wt% FeO compared to 8.1 wt% in underlying bedrock, exhibiting lower iron in 79% of windows (99.6% where bedrock is mafic) with virtually zero rank correlation (Spearman ρ = -0.02). Conversely, airborne thorium exceeds whole-rock thorium (9.4 vs. 5.1 ppm), reflecting chemical weathering that leaches mobile cations while concentrating thorium in resistate minerals. Among the 88 windows with all four elements measured on both tracks, whole rock satisfies all resource criteria for 25 of 59 lunar queries, whereas topsoil satisfies none. The terrestrial geochemical shortfall therefore stems from two distinct mechanisms: chemical weathering (limiting highland, low-Ti, and polar lunar analogs) and planetary petrogenesis (high-Ti mare basalts and iron-rich Martian crust, which are rare even in unweathered terrestrial rock). Earth lacks lunar-style ilmenite cumulates and Mars’s iron-rich mantle: 99.9% of 91,461 terrestrial basaltic analyses contain at most 5.6 wt% TiO₂, whereas Apollo 11 and 17 basalts exhibit mission medians of 11.2 and 12.1 wt%.

5.3 Sensitivity to Weights and Tolerances

Because no positive weighting scheme can fabricate a multi-property match where none exists, every query with an Earth ceiling below 1.0 remains below 1.0 across all 1,000 random Dirichlet weightings. While numeric ceiling values shift with weighting (lunar mean resource ceiling spans 0.63–0.97 between the 5th and 95th percentiles), even doubling all physical tolerances leaves two high-titanium lunar queries without any TiO₂ match and 47 of 52 Martian queries without any FeO match on Earth.

5.4 Heuristic Analogs vs. Property-Level Retrieval

Evaluated against a reference catalogue of 80 established analog sites, heuristic setting-based screening performed exactly as intended: a random top-30 draw from the screened pool contained expected-type catalogued analogs 12.2× more frequently than an unscreened random sample (95% CI: 7.0–19.1). However, when evaluated on independent physical and chemical measurements excluded from the screening rules, screened candidates were no closer to their planetary targets than random terrestrial windows (+1.3 percentage points; 95% CI: -3.2 to 5.2). At orbital gamma-ray scales, the trend reverses: for lunar and Martian targets, heuristically screened candidates matched footprint-scale K and Th 7.6 percentage points less often than random windows (13 of 13 pools negative)—a finding confirmed on the 80 random queries (-7.5 percentage points; all 20 distinct pools negative). An Earth-to-Earth positive control confirmed statistical sensitivity (+5.6 percentage points when querying terrestrial targets).

5.5 Spatial Predictability and the Extrapolation Frontier

Near measurements, terrestrial geochemistry is predictable. Within 300 km of calibration data, gradient-boosted trees achieved R² values of 0.64 (K), 0.41 (Th), 0.40 (FeO), and 0.32 (TiO₂), with 90% conformal intervals covering 90–93% of held-out windows—outperforming covariate nearest neighbours, inverse-distance weighting, and spatial Gaussian processes across all four targets. Across continents, extrapolation fails. Models trained on Australia and tested on North America (or vice versa) yielded negative R² across every element (-4.68 to -0.13). The cause is geological: deep, ancient weathering across the stable Australian craton leaches potassium while retaining thorium (median Th/K = 12.4 vs. 4.9 in North America), a regolith-age signal uncaptured by global surface covariates. Consequently, TwinGround restricts chemical predictions to within 300 km of measured ground and explicitly reports “no reliable estimate” beyond this boundary.

Spatial scale governs local analog availability. While 65% of covered Earth windows contain at least one 1 km cell matching some lunar query in airborne K and Th, this fraction drops to 41% at 8 km and 21% at 40 km, demonstrating that lunar-like geochemical patches exist locally on Earth but are diluted by orbital footprint averaging. Notably, such patches are absent at canonical lunar analog sites: within the Craters of the Moon and Meteor Crater windows, not a single 1 km cell matches any lunar query in both K and Th. Furthermore, kilometre-scale terrain morphology alone recovered at most two catalogued analogs across 31 queries, highlighting the resolution limits of current global planetary DEMs.

5.6 Mission Scenarios: Artemis South Pole and Jezero Crater

  • Artemis South Pole: Terrain and rover mobility rehearsals can utilize any terrestrial site matching kilometre-scale roughness. However, the polar illumination and thermal regime has no terrestrial counterpart: solar elevation never exceeds ≈ 7.5° above these windows, and permanently shadowed cold traps plunge to ≈ 25 K. Existing catalogued lunar analogs score at most 0.60 for this operational use (Nördlinger Ries, Lava Beds), while Craters of the Moon scores 0.
  • Jezero Crater: Regolith-scale resource ceilings peak at 0.57 (matching K and Th in southwestern Alaska and Saskatchewan, but falling short on FeO). Daytime surface temperature and albedo co-occur within tolerance across 3,864 terrestrial windows, 97% of which lie north of 50° N.

SysOne-Nano encodes a window once and evaluates multiple geological attributes in a single parallel pass. 7. System Architecture and Search Pipeline

Every planetary search—whether on the Moon or Mars—executes an identical, auditable five-stage pipeline:

  1. Ingest query window: Extract DEM grids (LOLA / SLDEM2015 for the Moon; MOLA and the HRSC-MOLA blend for Mars), 3D display meshes, and multi-instrument observational records.
  2. Global morphological scoring: Compute cosine similarity between the query’s terrain embedding and all indexed Earth windows at the matching spatial scale L.
  3. Purpose-driven re-scoring: Apply the selected mission purpose—evaluating ten-facet rules, user-defined environmental constraints, same-unit physical property matching, lava-tube proximity/morphology, or joint terrain + material similarity.
  4. Transparent context fusion: Combine scores using fixed, interpretable weights (without opaque learned rankers), apply optional visual re-ranking, and cluster adjacent high-scoring windows into distinct spatial candidate groups.
  5. Assemble evidence dossiers: Generate a structured evidence record for each spatial group containing measured/estimated property values with data provenance, condition verdicts, known-analog labels, logistics, climate profiles, and external NASA data links.

Dual Scoring Layers. Our underlying research study (§4–§5) evaluates four operational uses (resources, mobility, thermal environment, base siting) across eight harmonized physical properties, establishing the use score and the Earth ceiling. The live web application augments this foundation with a broader mission-planning layer: ten facets encompassing operational and environmental factors highlighted on the challenge page (such as sunlight, dust and wind, water and ice, and operations). The 0–100 score displayed on the results page (e.g., 81.2/100 in §9.5) reflects this ten-facet screening score and sits alongside—rather than replacing—the quantitative Earth ceiling (0.81 for the same query).

Ten Mission Facets. Every challenge consideration maps to a scored facet: (A) Terrain, (B) Surface Material, (C) Thermal, (D) Sunlight, (E) Water & Ice, (F) Dust & Wind, (G) Surface Processes, (H) Habitability, (I) Subsurface, and (J) Operations. Each facet averages its constituent tokens, scored as 1.0 (match), 0.5 (partial), 0 (mismatch), or unknown (missing Earth data, excluded from the denominator rather than penalized as zero). Each operational use applies a fixed weight vector over these facets, while physical parameters Earth cannot replicate anywhere (surface gravity, vacuum or thin atmosphere, surface radiation, and day–night cycle) are surfaced explicitly as hard physical limits.

Decoupled Assistant Service. The Ask assistant operates as an isolated microservice alongside the search engine. The web server serializes the active search state into a deterministic plain-text site brief and forwards it, along with dialogue history, to the model service on the same VM for passage retrieval and grounded generation (§9). The assistant reads search outputs but never modifies rankings or numerical values.

9. Site AI Assistant

Every page features an Ask button that opens an interactive AI assistant panel. The assistant answers questions regarding platform usage, scientific methodology, and underlying datasets. On the results page, users can toggle “Include the current candidate #1” to ask why a specific terrestrial site was selected—receiving a transparent breakdown of matched facets, partial matches, and properties Earth cannot replicate. Every answer cites numbered reference passages [n] and the live site record ([SITE], rendered in the UI as [candidate]), with clickable source cards displayed beneath the response for immediate verification. The assistant responds fluently in the user’s query language (English or Traditional Chinese) with full source attribution.

TwinGround enforces a strict architectural boundary: the language model explains; it never decides. All candidate rankings, facet scores, and numerical values originate from the deterministic search pipeline. The assistant receives these outputs purely as structured context and translates them into cited natural-language explanations.

9.1 Question-Answering Pipeline

  1. Request: The frontend transmits the dialogue history and, when active on the results page, the current search state to the backend server.
  2. Deterministic Site Brief: The backend serializes the search state into a structured plain-text site brief containing query coordinates and geology, measured properties, the Earth ceiling, non-reproducible planetary limits, ten-facet verdicts, same-unit property comparisons, GLiM lithology, nearest volcano/caldera, slope/roughness metrics, known-analog status, and competing candidates. No values are inferred by the LLM.
  3. Dense + Lexical Retrieval: The model service encodes the user’s query and retrieves top-matching passages from our curated corpus (§9.2).
  4. Grounded Generation: Our fine-tuned Llama 3.2 1B model synthesizes a concise, cited response from the retrieved passages and site brief. A post-processing filter strips any out-of-range citation indices prior to display.

9.2 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Corpus

  • Knowledge Corpus (1,553 passages): Comprises our research paper in English (116 passages) and Traditional Chinese (86), Supplementary Information in English (219) and Chinese (209), bilingual technical briefs, reliability and data-rights documentation, the project README, and UI documentation—augmented with 148 cited literature entries resolved via OpenAlex (including full-text passages for 8 open-access papers, totalling 551 passages).
  • Retriever: Uses Microsoft multilingual-e5-base dense embeddings (with "query:" and "passage:" prefixes and cosine similarity) combined with a lightweight lexical-overlap boost, passing the top 4 passages (or top 2 when a site brief is attached), capped at ≈ 2,600 characters, into the model context.

9.3 Synthetic Training Dataset: 10,220 Dialogues Distilled from a 70B Teacher

  • Real Search Scenarios: We executed 700 live searches across the server (55% Moon, 45% Mars; named and random targets; 20/40/80 km scales; all operational purposes), serializing the top 5 candidates per search into bilingual site briefs (7,000 site briefs total).
  • 70B Teacher Distillation: Using Meta Llama 3.3 70B Instruct served via vLLM across 8 × NVIDIA A100 40 GB GPUs, we generated training dialogues in three stages: (1) persona-driven question generation (student, mission planner, competition judge, ISRU engineer), (2) live retriever execution (deliberately withholding the seed passage in ≈ 15% of paper queries to teach calibrated abstention), and (3) grounded teacher responses adhering strictly to the student prompt format. An additional 2,400 follow-up turns were generated to support multi-turn dialogue coherence.
  • Quality Filtering: Automated checks enforced response length bounds, valid citation indices, target-language fidelity, zero Simplified Chinese characters, and strict refusal of ungrounded site claims. After discovering an 18% rate of unjustified “I don’t know” refusals in early Chinese site-brief answers (358 of 1,941), all false refusals on valid site briefs were purged prior to final training.

9.6 Production Serving

In production, the assistant runs as a dedicated local inference service alongside the web application on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU. Using greedy decoding capped at 450 new tokens, responses are returned in 2–4 seconds, consuming only ≈ 6.5 GB of total VRAM (including the web server and chat-search model). All inference executes self-hosted on our server—no user queries are transmitted to external third-party LLM APIs.

9.7 Known Assistant Limitations

  • Compact 1B models remain susceptible to occasional reasoning slips (e.g., inverting a temperature inequality or listing a partial facet under both matched and unmatched summaries); UI disclaimers prompt users to verify figures against the cited sources and results table.
  • Full-text retrieval spans the 8 open-access cited papers alongside our full technical documentation, while the remaining 140 cited works are indexed via bibliographic metadata.
  • The assistant serves strictly as an explanatory layer and cannot re-rank candidates or compute new geophysical measurements.

11. Benefits and Intended Impact

Core Benefits

  • From subjective appearance to quantitative equivalence: Ranks candidates using unit- and scale-harmonized physical measurements, boosting retrieval efficiency from -0.19–0.02 (qualitative screening) to 0.52–0.77.
  • Transparent physical boundaries: Quantifies the Earth ceiling upfront, alerting mission engineers to properties no terrestrial field site can supply so simulant and chamber testing can be budgeted early.
  • Full explainability and provenance: Details exact parameter matches, mismatches, and data sources for every candidate—reinforced by a citation-grounded bilingual AI assistant.
  • Global, fast exploration: Evaluates any coordinate across the Moon or Mars rather than restricting users to famous landmarks, powered by spatial grid indexing (8 s → 2 ms for 3,000 Lunar Prospector lookups).
  • Actionable field logistics: Equips mission planners with accessibility data, optimal seasonal weather windows, testable operations, and direct NASA Earthdata/Worldview links.
  • Open and reproducible science: Built exclusively on open datasets with SHA-256 pre-registered validation protocols and explicit source licensing.

Intended Impact

  • Enable evidence-based site selection: Empower Artemis and Mars mission planners, rover teams, and ISRU researchers to shortlist terrestrial analog sites backed by reproducible orbital-to-ground metrics rather than historical convention.
  • Establish a modular analog testing blueprint: Provide a clear boundary-condition inventory allocating terrain trials to field sites, feedstock chemistry to tailored simulants, and extreme thermal/vacuum testing to laboratory chambers.
  • Correct systematic selection biases: Alert the planetary science community to the continental-crust (high-K, high-Th) bias inherent in qualitative “dry basaltic” site screening.
  • Democratize planetary exploration: Allow students, educators, and the public worldwide to explore authentic NASA planetary data, ask questions in English or Traditional Chinese, master analog methodology via Game mode, and walk the Moon and Mars in 3D.

12. Technical Innovations & Creativity

  1. The Earth Ceiling Metric: Moves beyond relative candidate ranking to establish the upper bound of terrestrial similarity that any measured Earth window can reach for a planetary site, diagnosing whether limits arise from geochemistry, thermal/radiative regimes, or lack of parameter co-occurrence.
  2. Instrument-Convolved Spatial Matching: Bridges the scale gap between orbital gamma-ray spectrometers and terrestrial surveys by convolving Earth grids with instrument-specific response kernels (45 km Gaussian for Lunar Prospector; 220 km disk for Mars Odyssey) and analyzing scale dependence across a 1–40 km support ladder.
  3. Dual-Track Geochemical Separation: Evaluates regolith and bedrock tracks independently to disentangle terrestrial surface weathering effects from fundamental planetary differentiation.
  4. Uncertainty-Calibrated Scoring: Incorporates 90% conformal prediction intervals directly into match probabilities so interpolated estimates earn calibrated partial credit and are strictly masked beyond validated spatial bounds (300 km).
  5. Purpose-Specific Multi-Use Ranking: Dynamically re-weights physical properties and ten mission facets so the same lunar or Martian window yields tailored terrestrial analogs for ISRU resources, mobility, thermal environment, base siting, or lava-tube exploration.
  6. Pre-Registered Validation with Transparent Negative Results: Locks confirmatory test protocols via SHA-256 hashes prior to data inspection and explicitly integrates negative findings (cross-continental transfer failure, km-scale DEM limits) into system safeguards.
  7. Lightweight, Domain-Specific Neural Models: Combines a 6,424-parameter terrain encoder, a 171,522-parameter multimodal geological reader (SysOne-Nano), and a synthetically supervised skylight detector (F-Net v2)—all running on CPU and gated by frozen validation tests.
  8. Natural-Language Search Without Hallucinated Sites: Constrains our LoRA fine-tuned Llama 3.2 1B parser to emit closed-vocabulary JSON specs while keeping site ranking entirely deterministic and auditable.
  9. Citation-Grounded 1B Site Assistant: Distils 10,220 bilingual dialogues from a 70B teacher across 7,000 real site briefs and a live RAG retriever, enabling a 1B student model to explain complex trade-offs with 100% valid citations on 120 held-out dialogues.
  10. Edge-Efficient Production Footprint: Runs the chat parser and cited AI assistant within ≈ 6.5 GB VRAM on the single NVIDIA L4 GPU server that also hosts the web platform and geospatial index, with 2–4 s response latency.

13. Factors Considered and Limitations

  • Spatial Support and Sensing Depth: Orbital gamma-ray instruments sense the upper tens of centimetres integrated over tens to hundreds of kilometres; spatial scale is explicitly stated alongside every score.
  • Geochemical Data Coverage: High-resolution terrestrial topsoil and airborne radiometric surveys are concentrated in Australia, North America, and Europe; outside a 300 km radius of measurements, TwinGround explicitly reports “no reliable estimate” rather than extrapolating unreliably.
  • Weathering and Surface Occlusion: Regolith and bedrock are scored separately, while water bodies and dense vegetation (≥ 30% cover) that attenuate terrestrial gamma-ray signals are systematically masked.
  • Absolute Tolerance Calibration: Fixed physical tolerances (± 0.2 wt% K, ± 2 ppm Th) are relatively wide compared to ultra-low lunar and Martian baseline abundances, meaning Martian thorium matches cluster near the lower tail of terrestrial distributions.
  • Modelled Martian Temperatures: Because orbital thermal products lack synchronized overpass coverage, Martian surface temperatures rely on the Mars Climate Database (labelled as model outputs), and interactive base-siting scores gracefully fall back to roughness and albedo where thermal coverage is unavailable.
  • Licensing and Attribution: All datasets were audited for redistribution rights; proprietary display imagery (Esri World Imagery) is strictly isolated from analytical pipelines and visibly credited alongside third-party 3D assets.
  • Screening Scope: Ranked candidates represent quantitative screening leads rather than certified mission analog sites or traverse safety assessments. While the overarching Earth-ceiling framing was synthesized after inspecting experimental results, all underlying statistical protocols remained frozen and unmodified.
  • Compact LLM Guardrails: As a 1B-parameter model, the Site AI Assistant can occasionally misstate comparative inequalities; explicit UI notices encourage users to cross-check claims against the linked reference passages and results table (§9.7).

14. Conclusion

TwinGround transforms the qualitative question “Where on Earth resembles this location on the Moon or Mars?” into a rigorous, measurable engineering framework. By harmonizing NASA orbital observations and terrestrial surveys across units, spatial footprints, and sensing depths, the platform ranks terrestrial candidates for specific mission purposes, explains every match with verifiable citations, and establishes the Earth ceiling—the quantitative boundary of what Earth can replicate. Our findings demonstrate that while Earth readily provides kilometre-scale terrain analogs, it cannot replicate lunar mare geochemistry, iron-rich Martian regolith, extreme Martian nighttime cold, or lunar polar illumination—and that traditional setting-based site selection systematically drifts toward Earth’s continental crust. Ultimately, TwinGround delivers both a practical boundary-condition roadmap—allocating terrain validation to Earth field sites, geochemical testing to laboratory simulants, and extreme thermal regimes to thermal-vacuum chambers—and an accessible interactive platform with a bilingual assistant, empowering engineers, scientists, and students to explore authentic NASA planetary data.
